name: Vortex
tagline: Nexus Mods' official mod manager: installs, deploys and orders mods across hundreds of games.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified. Vortex itself is free; the money is the Nexus Mods membership that unlocks in-app downloads and ad-free browsing.

verdictSummary: The mechanical core of a mod manager is unglamorous and very buildable: extract archive into a staging folder, hardlink files into the game directory, keep a manifest of what came from where, report conflicts, write a load order file. For one game you play, an agent can get that working in a weekend and it will be faster and less opinionated than Vortex. What you cannot rebuild is the part you actually pay for: Nexus Mods hosting, the API that hands out download links to Premium members, and the nxm:// handoff from browser to manager. You also lose FOMOD scripted installers, LOOT-quality load order sorting, Collections, and the per-game knowledge baked into Vortex's extensions for hundreds of titles. Fine for a single stable Skyrim or Fallout setup, painful the moment you want a 300-mod list with conditional installers.
coreLoopDIY: Extracts mod archives into a staging tree, hardlinks them into the game folder with per-mod ownership tracking, and lets you enable, disable, order and cleanly uninstall from a CLI.
requirements: Local game install and mod archives you already downloaded
Staging folder on the same volume as the game so hardlinks work
Optional Nexus API key in .env for metadata lookups, and Premium if you want in-app download links
whatYouLose: One-click downloads from the mod site and browser nxm:// handoff
FOMOD and scripted installers, so conditional mods must be unpacked by hand
LOOT-grade load order sorting and conflict rules maintained by other people
Collections: someone else's tested 200-mod list installed in one go
Per-game support for hundreds of titles, plus a GUI your future self will thank you for
moatNotes: Vortex is a free client for a paid content network. The client is copyable; the mod library and its uploaders are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Nobody pays for Vortex, they pay Nexus Mods, and Vortex exists to make that membership feel worth it. The membership buys download speed, no ad wall, and the in-app download flow that makes a 200-mod list assembleable in an evening instead of a weekend of manual file shuffling. A DIY manager still points at the same servers and still respects the same rate limits, so you save nothing on the actual bottleneck. The honest DIY win is control: a small deterministic deploy tool you understand, on top of mods you already have on disk.
notes: Rebuilding the manager is a weekend; rebuilding the mod site is not the same project.
prompt:
Build a local, single-user game mod manager as a CLI tool. Empty folder, no cloud, no accounts, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Node 20 + TypeScript, ESM.
- commander for the CLI, better-sqlite3 for state, node:fs for deployment.
- 7-Zip via child_process for archive extraction (assume 7z is on PATH).
- vitest for tests.

Data model in SQLite (mods.db):
- mods: id, name, version, archive_path, staged_dir, enabled, priority, installed_at.
- files: mod_id, relative_path, deployed (bool), overwritten_by (nullable mod_id).
- profiles: id, name, active; profile_mods: profile_id, mod_id, enabled, priority.

Commands:
- init --game-dir PATH --staging PATH : validate both paths are on the same volume, warn loudly if not, store config in config.json.
- install ARCHIVE [--name] : extract into staging/<mod-id>/, detect and strip a redundant top-level Data or game-name folder, record the file list.
- enable NAME / disable NAME, priority NAME N.
- deploy : hardlink every file of every enabled mod into the game dir in priority order; on collision, the higher-priority mod wins and the loser is recorded in overwritten_by; back up any pre-existing vanilla file to a .vortexlike-backup sibling before overwriting.
- purge : remove all links this tool created, restore backups, leave the game dir vanilla. Must be exact, verified by the files table, never a recursive delete of the game dir.
- conflicts : print a table of file paths claimed by more than one enabled mod, with winner and losers.
- plugins : read and rewrite plugins.txt for a Bethesda-style game, ordering .esp/.esm/.esl by mod priority, preserving manual pins from a plugins.pins file.
- profile create/switch/list.

Rules:
- Every destructive command supports --dry-run and prints exactly what it would do.
- Deployment is idempotent: running deploy twice changes nothing.
- Config and any Nexus API key live in .env / config.json, never hardcoded. If NEXUS_API_KEY is set, add a metadata NAME command that fetches mod name and version only; do not attempt downloads.

Explicitly out of scope: GUI, FOMOD/scripted installers, LOOT-style rule sorting, collections, nxm:// protocol handling, multi-game extension system. Support exactly one game, configured at init.

Deliver: src/, a README with a five-line quickstart, and vitest tests covering collision resolution, idempotent deploy, and a purge that provably restores the original file set.
